name: Corpus callosum
func: The largest bundle of nerve fibers in the brain, a thick C-shaped bridge joining the left and right hemispheres. It lets the two halves share information so they work as one brain.

levels.kid:
Your brain has two halves, a left half and a right half. They need to talk to each other all the time!

The **corpus callosum** is the big **bridge** in the middle that connects them. It is made of millions and millions of tiny wires.

When your left hand feels something soft, the right half of your brain feels it first. Then it sends the news across the bridge so the left half knows too, and the left half can help you say the word "soft."

Thanks to this bridge, both halves work together like a team, like two hands clapping.
levels.hs:
The **corpus callosum** ("tough body") is the largest **commissure**, a fiber bundle that crosses the midline to connect the two cerebral hemispheres. It contains roughly 200 million axons. It lies at the bottom of the **longitudinal fissure**, the deep groove between the hemispheres, so you see it clearly when the brain is cut down the middle. Above it lies the **cingulate gyrus**, and below it are the **lateral ventricles**, which it roofs. The **septum pellucidum**, a thin membrane between the two lateral ventricles, hangs down from its underside, and the **fornix** curves beneath its back half.

From front to back it has four parts:

- **Rostrum:** the thin tip curving back under the front.
- **Genu** ("knee"): the bend at the front, connecting the frontal lobes.
- **Body (trunk):** the long middle section, connecting frontal and parietal areas.
- **Splenium:** the thick rounded back end, connecting the occipital and temporal lobes, so it carries a lot of visual information.

The corpus callosum mostly connects matching areas on the two sides. It is especially important when information that reaches only one hemisphere must be used by the other. For example, language is usually in the left hemisphere, so naming an object felt only by the left hand requires the message to cross the corpus callosum.
levels.college:
**Fiber topography:** genu fibers connect prefrontal cortex and curve forward as the **forceps minor**; body fibers connect premotor, motor, somatosensory and parietal areas; and splenium fibers connect occipital and posterior temporal cortex, curving backward as the **forceps major**. The **tapetum**, made of body and splenium fibers, forms the roof and lateral wall of the temporal horn and atrium of the lateral ventricle. Witelson's scheme divides the body into thirds and a posterior "isthmus"; DTI studies refine the map (Hofer and Frahm), placing motor fibers more posteriorly than older schemes.

**Homotopic and heterotopic:** most fibers link matching areas (homotopic); some connect different regions. Primary sensory areas for the hands and feet and much of primary visual cortex have relatively few callosal connections, except along the vertical midline of the visual field, which helps fuse the two visual half-fields seamlessly.

**Other commissures:** the **anterior commissure** (connecting temporal lobes and olfactory regions), the **hippocampal commissure** (between the crura of the fornix), and the posterior commissure.

**Blood supply:** the **pericallosal artery**, a branch of the ACA, runs along its upper surface and supplies most of it. The splenium also receives branches from the **posterior pericallosal (splenial) artery** of the PCA. The dual supply makes callosal infarcts uncommon.

**Development:** the corpus callosum forms between about 12 and 20 weeks of development before birth, generally front to back (genu and body before splenium), with the rostrum forming last. Glial "guidepost" structures such as the **indusium griseum glia** and **glial wedge** help axons cross, using guidance molecules such as Slit/Robo and netrin. Myelination continues through adolescence.
levels.phd:
**Fiber composition:** most callosal axons are small and thinly myelinated or unmyelinated, with the largest, fastest fibers in the regions connecting motor and sensory areas. This gives interhemispheric conduction delays of a few milliseconds for large fibers to tens of milliseconds for small ones. It has been argued that conduction delays in larger brains favor hemispheric specialization, since crossing becomes slower (Ringo and colleagues).

**Excitation and inhibition:** callosal axons are glutamatergic and excitatory, but they often activate inhibitory interneurons on the other side, producing **interhemispheric inhibition**. TMS studies show that stimulating one motor cortex briefly suppresses the opposite one, which helps keep the two hands moving independently. Mirror movements in young children reflect immature interhemispheric inhibition.

**Split-brain research:** Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga studied patients whose corpus callosum had been cut to control severe epilepsy (Sperry, Nobel Prize 1981). When an image was flashed to only the left visual field, reaching only the right hemisphere, patients could not name it, but could pick it out with the left hand. Gazzaniga described a left-hemisphere **"interpreter"** that invents explanations for behaviors started by the right hemisphere.

**Agenesis of the corpus callosum** occurs in roughly 1 in 4,000 births. Strikingly, many people born without it do not show the classic disconnection signs. Possible reasons include **Probst bundles**, misrouted callosal axons running front to back on each side, and compensatory use of other commissures. MRI studies show reorganized connectivity, including some interhemispheric functional coupling. Outcomes range from typical development to significant disability, depending on associated brain differences and genetic causes.
levels.expert:
**Disconnection syndromes:**

- **Alexia without agraphia:** a left PCA stroke destroys left visual cortex and the **splenium**. Visual information from the intact right occipital lobe cannot reach the left-hemisphere language areas, so the patient can write but not read.
- **Left-hand tactile anomia and apraxia:** with damage to the anterior or middle corpus callosum, the left hand cannot name objects it feels or carry out commands.
- **Alien hand syndrome:** the **callosal variant** involves intermanual conflict, in which the left hand acts against the right (e.g., one hand buttons a shirt while the other unbuttons it). A frontal variant involves the SMA and medial frontal cortex.

**Diseases and imaging findings:**

- **Multiple sclerosis:** ovoid lesions at the **callososeptal interface**, perpendicular to the ventricles (**Dawson's fingers**), are characteristic on sagittal FLAIR MRI.
- **Diffuse axonal injury:** shearing forces from rapid acceleration or rotation (e.g., car crashes) cause hemorrhagic lesions, with the **splenium** a common site; susceptibility-weighted MRI is most sensitive.
- **Glioblastoma and CNS lymphoma** can spread across the corpus callosum to both hemispheres, creating a **"butterfly" lesion**.
- **Cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum (CLOCCs)**: reversible splenial lesions linked to seizures, infections or certain medications.
- **Susac syndrome**: central callosal "snowball" lesions with hearing loss and retinal artery occlusions.

**Surgery:** **corpus callosotomy**, cutting the anterior two-thirds or all of the corpus callosum, is used for drug-resistant epilepsy with **drop attacks** (atonic seizures), often in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. The **transcallosal approach** through a small callosal opening reaches tumors and cysts of the lateral and third ventricles (for example colloid cysts) while protecting the pericallosal arteries.

keyPoints: Roofs the lateral ventricles; cingulate gyrus lies above
Supplied mainly by the pericallosal artery (ACA)
Splenium + left visual cortex lesion → alexia without agraphia
Callosotomy treats drop attacks; split-brain studies by Sperry

test.q: Which part of the corpus callosum connects the occipital lobes?
test.explain: The splenium carries visual fibers, curving back as the forceps major.

test.q: The ACA branch running along the top of the corpus callosum is the ______ artery.
test.explain: It supplies most of the corpus callosum.

test.q: A patient can write a sentence but cannot read it back after a left PCA stroke. Which part of the corpus callosum was also damaged?
test.explain: Alexia without agraphia results from left occipital plus splenial damage.

test.q: In a split-brain patient, an object felt only by the left hand cannot be named because:
choices: The left hand has no sensation
Touch information reaches the right hemisphere but cannot cross to the left-hemisphere language areas
test.explain: Left-hand touch goes to the right hemisphere; language is usually left-sided.

test.q: Who won the 1981 Nobel Prize for split-brain research?
test.explain: Sperry worked with Gazzaniga on callosotomy patients.

test.q: Ovoid MS lesions perpendicular to the ventricles at the callososeptal interface are called:
test.explain: Dawson's fingers are typical of multiple sclerosis on sagittal FLAIR.
